los.text: Explain the main causes, signs and symptoms and investigations in a patient presenting with ocular complaint (visual loss, field loss, ocular trauma, double vision)
los.html:
ComplaintKey causes
Sudden painless visual loss
  • Central retinal artery occlusion (cherry-red spot, pale retina; check for GCA/emboli)
  • Retinal vein occlusion ("stormy sunset" haemorrhages)
  • Vitreous haemorrhage (diabetes)
  • Retinal detachment (flashes, floaters, curtain)
  • Wet AMD
  • GCA (AION; jaw claudication, scalp tenderness → urgent ESR/CRP + steroids)
  • Stroke/TIA (amaurosis fugax)
Sudden painful visual lossAcute angle-closure glaucoma, optic neuritis (pain on eye movement), keratitis, uveitis, endophthalmitis
Gradual visual lossCataract, dry AMD, open-angle glaucoma (peripheral first), diabetic maculopathy, refractive error
Field lossGlaucoma (arcuate), retinal detachment, chiasmal compression (bitemporal), stroke (homonymous)
Double visionMonocular (cataract, refractive) vs binocular (CN III (surgical third: pupil involved → aneurysm), IV, VI palsies; myasthenia; thyroid eye disease; orbital fracture; INO in MS)
Ocular traumaBlunt (hyphaema, orbital blowout fracture: restricted upgaze, diplopia, infraorbital numbness), penetrating (irregular pupil → shield, no pressure, urgent ophthalmology), chemical injury (irrigate immediately, check pH)
  • Investigations/exam: visual acuity (Snellen, pinhole)
    • pupils (RAPD)
    • fields (confrontation)
    • colour vision (Ishihara: optic neuritis)
    • eye movements
    • fundoscopy (red reflex)
    • slit lamp
    • fluorescein
    • IOP (tonometry)
    • OCT, fluorescein angiography, visual field perimetry
    • CT orbit (trauma), MRI (optic neuritis, chiasm), ESR/CRP (GCA), glucose, BP.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat acute eye conditions and glaucoma and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Drug classExampleMechanismUse / cautions
Prostaglandin analoguesLatanoprost↑ uveoscleral outflow1st line POAG; iris darkening, lash growth, periorbital fat loss
β-blockersTimolol↓ aqueous production (ciliary body)Systemic absorption → bronchospasm, bradycardia: avoid in asthma/heart block
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitorsDorzolamide (topical), acetazolamide (oral/IV)↓ aqueous productionAcetazolamide: paraesthesia, ↓K⁺, sulfonamide allergy
α2 agonistsBrimonidine↓ production, ↑ outflowAllergy; avoid in infants
Miotics (cholinergic)PilocarpineConstricts pupil → opens angle, ↑ trabecular outflowAcute angle closure (after IOP lowered)
MydriaticsTropicamide (antimuscarinic), phenylephrine (α1)Dilate pupilFundoscopy; can precipitate angle closure
CycloplegicsCyclopentolate, atropineParalyse ciliary muscleUveitis (pain relief, prevents synechiae)
Topical steroidsPrednisolone acetate, dexamethasoneAnti-inflammatoryAnterior uveitis, post-op; risk ↑ IOP, cataract, worsen herpetic keratitis (never without ophthalmology)
AntibioticsChloramphenicol, fusidic acid; ofloxacin (contact lens)Bacterial conjunctivitis, keratitis
AntiviralsTopical aciclovir/ganciclovirHSV dendritic ulcer
Anti-VEGF (intravitreal)Ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimabBlock VEGF → ↓ neovascularisation/leakWet AMD, diabetic macular oedema, RVO
Antihistamines/mast cell stabilisersOlopatadine, sodium cromoglicateAllergic conjunctivitis
Acute angle-closure glaucomaIV acetazolamide + topical pilocarpine, β-blocker, α-agonist, ± IV mannitol; analgesia/antiemetic; definitive laser peripheral iridotomy (both eyes).
Open-angle glaucomaProstaglandin analogue first line (NICE also supports selective laser trabeculoplasty first), then add others; trabeculectomy.

los.text: Describe the common aetiologies, presenting symptoms, and basic diagnostic approaches for a patient presenting with a red eye
los.html:
CausePainVisionFeatures
Conjunctivitis (bacterial, viral, allergic)Gritty/itchy, not painfulNormalDiffuse redness, discharge (purulent: bacterial; watery + preauricular nodes: viral (adenovirus); itchy + bilateral: allergic)
Subconjunctival haemorrhageNoneNormalBright red patch; check BP/INR
EpiscleritisMildNormalSectoral, blanches with phenylephrine
ScleritisSevere, boring, wakes at night↓Associated RA/vasculitis; urgent
Anterior uveitis (iritis)Painful, photophobia↓Ciliary flush, small/irregular pupil, hypopyon; HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis, IBD)
Keratitis (bacterial, HSV, Acanthamoeba)Painful, FB sensation, photophobia↓Contact lens wearers; fluorescein: corneal ulcer, dendritic ulcer (HSV)
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere, headache, vomiting↓, haloesFixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, rock-hard eye; hypermetropes, elderly, dim light/mydriatics
Corneal abrasion / foreign bodyPainful±Fluorescein staining; evert lid
EndophthalmitisPainful↓↓After surgery/injection; emergency
Red flags(urgent ophthalmology)Reduced vision, significant pain, photophobia, abnormal pupil, corneal opacity/staining, contact lens wearer, recent surgery/trauma, chemical injury.
ApproachHistory (onset, unilateral/bilateral, pain, discharge, vision, contact lenses, trauma, systemic disease), acuity, pupils, fluorescein, pattern of redness, IOP.

los.text: Describe the clinical signs and symptoms, and pathophysiology of common eye diseases (glaucoma, macular degeneration, cataract and retinal disease)
los.html:
Glaucoma
  • Progressive optic neuropathy (cupping: ↑ cup-to-disc ratio >0.6, notching) with characteristic field loss, usually with ↑ IOP (normal 10–21 mmHg).
  • Primary open-angle: ↓ trabecular meshwork outflow; asymptomatic, peripheral (arcuate) field loss → tunnel vision. Risk: age, FHx, Black ethnicity, myopia, diabetes. Screened by optometrists.
  • Acute angle-closure: iris blocks drainage angle → rapid IOP rise (>40–60 mmHg).
Age-related macular degeneration(commonest cause of blindness in UK elderly)
  • Dry (~90%; drusen, geographic atrophy, gradual central loss) vs wet/neovascular (choroidal neovascularisation → leakage, haemorrhage → rapid distortion (metamorphopsia: Amsler grid), central scotoma; anti-VEGF).
  • Risk: age, smoking, FHx, white ethnicity.
Cataract
  • Lens opacification (protein denaturation/oxidation): age (nuclear sclerosis), diabetes, steroids, UV, smoking, trauma, congenital (rubella).
  • Gradual blurred vision, glare, faded colours, ↓ red reflex.
  • Rx: phacoemulsification + intraocular lens.
Retinal disease
  • Diabetic retinopathy (see week 139).
  • Hypertensive retinopathy: arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, papilloedema (malignant HTN).
  • Retinal detachment: rhegmatogenous (tear → fluid under retina): flashes, floaters, shadow/curtain; risk: myopia, trauma, cataract surgery → urgent surgery (especially macula-on).
  • Retinal artery/vein occlusion (see LO 1); retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness, tunnel vision, bone-spicule pigment).

los.text: Describe the principles and structures involved in the process of vision refraction and physiology of the anterior segment of the eye
los.html:
RefractionLight is bent mainly by the cornea (~⅔, ~43 D) and the lens (~⅓, adjustable) to focus on the retina (fovea).
Accommodation(near vision)
  • Ciliary muscle contracts (parasympathetic, CN III via ciliary ganglion, M3) → zonules relax → lens becomes more convex (↑ power)
  • Plus pupil constriction and convergence (near triad).
Refractive errors
  • Myopia (short-sighted): eyeball too long/power too strong → image in front of retina → concave (minus) lens.
  • Hypermetropia (long-sighted): eye too short → image behind retina → convex (plus) lens; ↑ risk angle closure.
  • Astigmatism: unequal corneal curvature → cylindrical lens.
  • Presbyopia: age-related loss of lens elasticity → ↓ accommodation (from ~40s) → reading glasses.
Anterior segment
  • Cornea (avascular, transparent: regular collagen lamellae, endothelial pump keeps it dehydrated; densely innervated by CN V1)
  • Anterior chamber and aqueous humour
  • Iris
  • Drainage angle
  • Lens
  • Ciliary body.
Aqueous humour
  • Produced by ciliary body epithelium (carbonic anhydrase, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; β-adrenergic stimulation)
  • → posterior chamber
  • → through pupil
  • → anterior chamber
  • → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm (~80–90%) or uveoscleral outflow (~10–20%).
  • Nourishes cornea and lens
  • Maintains IOP.
Pupil
  • Sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic) constricts
  • Dilator pupillae (sympathetic, α1) dilates.
  • Pupillary light reflex: afferent CN II → pretectal nucleus → bilateral Edinger–Westphal → efferent CN III (direct + consensual).

los.text: Describe the neural pathways that convey visual information to the cerebral cortex for image perception, and explain the effects of various lesions on the visual field
sessions: BMS 2: Visual pathway and field defects
los.html:
• Pathway: retina
    • → optic nerve
    • → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross = temporal visual fields)
    • → optic tract
    • → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus)
    • → optic radiations (Meyer's loop through temporal lobe = superior fields; parietal fibres = inferior fields)
    • → primary visual cortex (occipital, calcarine sulcus; macula at occipital pole; supplied by PCA with MCA collateral at pole).
Lesion siteField defectTypical cause
Optic nerveMonocular loss/central scotoma, RAPDOptic neuritis, AION, compression, glaucoma
Optic chiasm (central)Bitemporal hemianopiaPituitary adenoma (upper quadrants first), craniopharyngioma (lower first)
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia (incongruous)Tumour, stroke
Temporal radiations (Meyer's loop)Contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")Temporal lobe lesion (stroke, tumour, surgery)
Parietal radiationsContralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor")Parietal lesion
Occipital cortexContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (congruous)PCA stroke
Mnemonic"PITS" (Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior).
AssessmentConfrontation fields, formal perimetry; check for visual inattention (parietal neglect) separately.

los.text: Describe the basic function and visual processing pathway of the eye
los.html:
Eye layersOuter fibrous (sclera, cornea), middle vascular uvea (choroid, ciliary body, iris), inner retina.
Retina
  • Light passes through inner layers to photoreceptors (outermost, next to RPE).
  • Rods (~120 million; peripheral; very sensitive, scotopic/night vision, rhodopsin, no colour, low acuity) and cones (~6 million; concentrated in fovea; photopic, colour (S, M, L opsins), high acuity).
  • Optic disc = blind spot (no photoreceptors).
Phototransduction
  • Light
  • → 11-cis retinal → all-trans (rhodopsin activated)
  • → transducin
  • → PDE ↑
  • → ↓ cGMP
  • → cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels close
  • → photoreceptor hyperpolarises
  • → ↓ glutamate release (in dark, photoreceptors are depolarised: "dark current").
  • Vitamin A deficiency → night blindness.
Retinal processing
  • Photoreceptors
  • → bipolar cells (ON and OFF)
  • → ganglion cells (axons = optic nerve), with lateral modulation by horizontal and amacrine cells (centre–surround receptive fields → edge/contrast detection).
  • Convergence in periphery (sensitivity) vs 1:1 in fovea (acuity).
Ganglion cell typesParvocellular (P; colour, fine detail) and magnocellular (M; motion, contrast) streams → LGN layers → V1.
Cortical processingV1 (orientation, edges; ocular dominance columns) → dorsal stream (parietal: "where/how": motion, spatial location) and ventral stream (temporal: "what": object/face recognition; lesions → visual agnosia, prosopagnosia).
Other pathwaysPretectal (pupillary reflex), superior colliculus (saccades/orienting), suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian rhythm).
